Also, because they are asking for it and my mom raised me that you tip everybody. I've curbed it a lot since my europe trip, but I still tip $0.50 at a coffee shop if I order multiple things.

For those that do not receive a tipping wage, you are generally tipping to ensure a certain quality of service or to compensate for charges or fees that go directly to the employer or expenses directly incurred by the employee.

For the valet, doormen and the like, you are making sure that the next time you use the services, you will receive quick attention. With valet, the amount of your tip may mean your vehicle is parked closer to the valet stand resulting in quick retrieval when you are ready to go. The doormen might rush to have the door open for you when they see you approaching, help you carry something inside or hail a cab for you.

For drivers, that aren't wholly independent contractors, they probably work for some sort of agency or service, which owns the vehicles and takes a good portion of the total amount you pay. The drivers may be responsible for paying for their own gas, insurance and other incidental costs. Your tips help offset those costs. Tipping a driver can also have the same impact as it would for the valet or doorman. You could tell a driver during your trip, "$10 extra if you get me there as quick as you can." Another example would be tipping well and getting the drivers contact information. You can then call the driver before you are ready to leave, and the driver will happily return and wait for you, without the need for you to wait at a taxi stand or try and hail a cab. This works really well at concerts and other instances where there are masses of people trying to get a ride.

You may think that this only works in those situations where you see the same driver/valet/etc repeatedly, but keep in mind that information travels (as you noted in your post). A big tip to a doorman might mean a bartender gives you prompt service, no or low tip might mean everyone in the establishment avoids you.
